questions.q: What is the steric number and electron-pair geometry of the sulfite ion, SO₃²⁻?
questions.a: Steric number = 4 (three S–O bonding domains + one lone pair on S); electron-pair geometry = tetrahedral. A wrong answer (e.g., steric number 3, trigonal planar) reveals the student forgot to include the lone pair on sulfur or miscounted valence electrons (S:6, O:6×3=18, charge:+2 → total 26 e⁻; after three S–O bonds and octets on O, 2 e⁻ remain as a lone pair on S).

questions.q: Explain why the bond angle in NH₃ (107°) is smaller than the ideal tetrahedral angle (109.5°) but larger than the H–O–H angle in H₂O (104.5°).
questions.a: NH₃ has one lone pair (lp–bp repulsion compresses angles from 109.5° to ~107°); H₂O has two lone pairs (lp–lp repulsion > lp–bp, so greater compression to ~104.5°). A wrong answer (e.g., "both have one lone pair" or "electronegativity difference") reveals confusion between number of lone pairs and the repulsion hierarchy (lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp).

questions.q: Predict the molecular geometry and approximate bond angles for ClF₃. Show your reasoning stepwise.
questions.a: Step 1: Valence electrons = Cl(7) + 3×F(7) = 28 e⁻. Step 2: Lewis structure → Cl central, three Cl–F bonds, two lone pairs on Cl (3 bonding + 2 lone = 5 domains). Step 3: Steric number 5 → trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry. Step 4: Lone pairs occupy equatorial positions (minimizing lp–lp and lp–bp repulsions). Step 5: Molecular shape = T-shaped. Step 6: Equatorial F–Cl–F angle < 120° (lp–bp repulsion), axial F–Cl–F angle = 180° (ideal). Wrong answer (e.g., trigonal planar) reveals failure to place lone pairs in equatorial sites or misapplication of steric number.

questions.q: Compare the molecular geometries of XeF₂ and XeF₄. Why are both nonpolar despite having lone pairs?
questions.a: XeF₂: steric number 5 (2 bp + 3 lp) → linear molecular geometry (lone pairs equatorial). XeF₄: steric number 6 (4 bp + 2 lp) → square planar (lone pairs axial). Both are nonpolar because individual bond dipoles cancel symmetrically (linear: equal and opposite; square planar: four dipoles at 90° cancel in pairs). A wrong answer (e.g., "XeF₂ is bent") reveals ignorance of lone-pair positioning rules in trigonal bipyramidal/octahedral geometries.

questions.q: A student claims: "In PF₅, all P–F bond lengths are equal because the molecule is trigonal bipyramidal." Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is false. In trigonal bipyramidal PF₅, axial P–F bonds are longer (more repulsion from three equatorial bp at 90°) than equatorial P–F bonds (repulsion from two axial bp at 90°). Experimental data: axial ~158 pm, equatorial ~153 pm. A wrong evaluation (agreeing) reveals the student thinks "trigonal bipyramidal" implies equivalence of all positions, ignoring the distinction between axial and equatorial sites.

questions.q: Design a VSEPR-based argument to predict whether the hypothetical ion ICl₄⁻ would be square planar or tetrahedral. Justify your prediction with electron-domain counting and lone-pair placement.
questions.a: Valence electrons: I(7) + 4×Cl(7) + 1(charge) = 36 e⁻. Lewis structure: I central, four I–Cl bonds, two lone pairs on I → 6 electron domains (steric number 6). Electron geometry = octahedral. Two lone pairs occupy opposite (axial) positions to minimize lp–lp repulsion (180° apart). Molecular geometry = square planar. A poor answer (e.g., "tetrahedral because four bonds") reveals failure to count lone pairs on the central atom or to apply octahedral lone-pair placement rule.
